title: Strict vs non-strict inequalities in continuous vs discrete distributions
scenario_markdown: A quality engineering team evaluates inequality boundaries across two settings: (1) component operating lifetime $X$ in hours, which is continuous ($X \sim N(100, 10^2)$), and (2) the number of defective parts $Y$ in a batch of 10 items, which is discrete ($Y \sim \text{Binomial}(n = 10, p = 0.2)$).
assumptions: Continuous random variables have P(X = c) = 0 for any single point c
Discrete random variables have P(Y = k) > 0 for integer values k in their support

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: for continuous X, P(X <= c) = P(X < c) + P(X = c) = P(X < c) + 0. For discrete Y ~ Binomial(10, 0.2), P(Y < 2) = P(Y <= 1) = 0.3758 != P(Y <= 2) = 0.6778 because P(Y = 2) = 0.3020.

stages.prompt_markdown: For the continuous lifespan $X \sim N(100, 10^2)$, how does $P(X \le 100)$ compare to the strict inequality $P(X < 100)$?

options.text_markdown: $P(X \le 100) = P(X < 100) = 0.5000$ exactly, because the individual point $P(X = 100) = 0$.
$P(X \le 100)$ is strictly greater than $P(X < 100)$ because it includes the median value $100$.
options.hint_markdown: In any continuous distribution, single points have zero width and zero probability: $P(X = 100) = 0$.

options.text_markdown: $P(X < 100)$ must be approximated by adding or subtracting $0.5$ as a continuity correction.
options.hint_markdown: A continuity correction is only used when approximating a discrete variable with a continuous one, not when working with an inherently continuous variable.

stages.explanation_markdown: Because $X$ is continuous, the probability of any individual point is zero ($P(X = 100) = 0$). By the addition rule for disjoint events, $P(X \le 100) = P(X < 100) + P(X = 100) = P(X < 100) + 0 = 0.5000$. Including or excluding boundary points never changes continuous probabilities.

stages.prompt_markdown: For the discrete defect count $Y \sim \text{Binomial}(10, 0.2)$, how does $P(Y < 2)$ compare to $P(Y \le 2)$?

options.text_markdown: $P(Y < 2) = P(Y \le 1) \approx 0.3758$, which is strictly less than $P(Y \le 2) \approx 0.6778$ by exactly $P(Y = 2) \approx 0.3020$.
$P(Y < 2) = P(Y \le 2)$, because the strictness of inequalities does not affect probability calculations.
options.hint_markdown: In discrete distributions, $P(Y = 2) > 0$. Therefore, $P(Y \le 2) = P(Y < 2) + P(Y = 2) > P(Y < 2)$.
Calculate $P(Y \le 1) = P(Y=0) + P(Y=1)$ vs. $P(Y \le 2) = P(Y \le 1) + P(Y=2)$.

stages.explanation_markdown: In discrete distributions, individual integers carry non-zero probability mass: $P(Y = 2) = \binom{10}{2}(0.2)^2(0.8)^8 \approx 0.3020$. Therefore, $P(Y < 2) = P(Y \le 1) = \text{BINOM.DIST}(1, 10, 0.2, \text{TRUE}) \approx 0.3758$, while $P(Y \le 2) = \text{BINOM.DIST}(2, 10, 0.2, \text{TRUE}) \approx 0.6778$. The boundary value makes a substantial difference.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which general principle summarizes the role of boundary points in continuous vs discrete probability?

options.text_markdown: For continuous variables, endpoints do not matter ($P(a < X < b) = P(a \le X \le b)$); for discrete variables, endpoints must be handled with strict precision because $P(Y = k) > 0$.
Endpoints always matter equally in both continuous and discrete distributions.
options.hint_markdown: In continuous distributions, area over a single point is zero, so including the point adds zero area.

options.text_markdown: Endpoints never matter in either distribution once sample size exceeds 30.
options.hint_markdown: Sample size does not alter the fundamental definition of discrete random variables.

stages.explanation_markdown: A core invariant of probability: In continuous distributions, $P(a < X < b) = P(a \le X < b) = P(a < X \le b) = P(a \le X \le b)$ because $P(X = a) = P(X = b) = 0$. In discrete distributions, boundary points carry non-zero probability mass, so $P(Y < k) = P(Y \le k - 1) \ne P(Y \le k)$.
